articleHeader.title: Comments in C — More Than Just // and /* */
articleHeader.subtitle: Comments look trivial until they silently break your build, get stripped by the preprocessor, or fail on a compiler you didn't test against. Here's what actually trips people up.

sections.title: What Are Comments in C, Really?

blocks.text: A comment in C is text the preprocessor deletes before the compiler ever sees it — not text the compiler ignores. That distinction matters more than most tutorials admit. Run gcc -E hello.c on a file full of comments and you'll see them vanish from the output entirely, replaced by nothing (or, in some GCC versions, a single space). By the time the actual compilation phase starts, your comments don't exist as tokens at all.

C gives you exactly two comment forms: the block comment /* ... */, which has existed since K&R C in 1978, and the line comment //, which was borrowed from C++ and only became official in the C99 standard — 21 years later. If you've only ever compiled with a modern GCC or Clang, that gap won't have bitten you. It bites people the day they touch an embedded compiler that still targets C89.

sections.title: Single-Line vs Multi-Line — Syntax and When to Use Each

blocks.label: comments.c
lines: * Converts a temperature reading from the DHT22 sensor
* Formula taken from DHT22 datasheet section 6.2.
int reading = 512; // sample value logged at 06:40 AM test run

blocks.text: Notice the split in that example: the block comment explains the intent and cites where the formula came from — the kind of thing future-you will thank past-you for — while the line comment notes a fact specific to that exact line (the hardware constants). That's the practical rule I actually follow: block comments for 'why this function exists', line comments for 'why this particular number is what it is'.

sections.title: The Nesting Trap — Why /* */ Inside /* */ Silently Breaks

blocks.text: I once spent close to forty minutes debugging a function that appeared to do nothing, because I'd commented out a block during testing and forgotten it contained another block comment. C does not support nested /* */ comments. The compiler closes the comment at the first */ it finds, no matter how many /* came before it.

blocks.label: nesting-bug.c
lines: for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) sum += data[i];
return 0;   // this line is now OUTSIDE the comment — it compiles fine,
// but everything above 'replace with CRC32 later */' is live code again

blocks.text: The outer /* closes at the first */ — right after 'replace with CRC32 later'. Everything from int sum = 0; onward becomes real, active code again, sitting outside any function. GCC will not stay quiet about this; you'll get something like error: expected identifier or '(' before 'int' pointing at a line that looks completely innocent to you, because the actual problem is several lines above it.

The fix I use in practice: never comment out a block that itself has comments in it. Wrap it with #if 0 ... #endif instead — the preprocessor handles nesting correctly because it's tracking directives, not comment delimiters.

sections.title: The C90 Trap: When // Comments Refuse to Compile

blocks.text: Line comments feel so universal today that it's easy to forget they're a C99 addition. Compile the same file with strict old-standard flags and GCC turns on you:

blocks.label: terminal
lines: sensor.c:9:20: error: C++ style comments are not allowed in ISO C90
sensor.c:9:20: error: (this will be reported only once per input file)

blocks.text: This exact message is worth memorizing if you ever touch legacy automotive or industrial C codebases still pinned to -std=c89 for MISRA-C compliance. Without -pedantic-errors, GCC will usually accept // anyway (as a compiler extension) and just move on — which means the bug won't show up until someone runs the project's official build with strict flags, often in CI, not on your machine.

sections.title: Comment Syntax Across Languages — Quick Reference

blocks.text: Useful if you're switching between C and other languages in the same week — the block-comment syntax in particular is not as universal as people assume.

That 'Nestable? — Yes' cell for Rust is not a footnote to skip past. It's the single biggest quality-of-life difference between commenting out a block in Rust versus doing the same thing in C, and it's exactly the gap that causes the bug described above.

sections.title: Doxygen-Style Comments — Turning Comments Into Documentation

blocks.text: C has no built-in documentation-comment syntax the way Java has Javadoc, but the de-facto convention — used across most open-source C projects including large chunks of the Linux kernel's driver subsystem — is Doxygen style: an extra * or ! after the opening delimiter, plus @param / @return tags.

blocks.label: doxygen-example.c
lines: * @brief Clamp a PWM duty-cycle value to the safe range for the L298N driver.
* @return Clamped value guaranteed to be within [0, 200] — values above
*         200 caused audible whine on Rev-B boards during bring-up testing.

blocks.text: That comment does something a bare // clamp value never could: it records why the upper bound is 200 and not 255, which is the actual knowledge worth preserving. Running doxygen on a codebase using this style generates browsable HTML API docs automatically — no separate documentation effort required.

items.text: — `i++; // increment i` wastes a line explaining syntax the reader already knows. Reserve comments for the reasoning the code itself can't show, like why a magic number is 200 and not 255.

items.strong: Delete dead code, don't comment it out
items.text: — In a ~12,000-line automotive telemetry codebase I worked on, a source-control audit found that roughly a third of all `/* */` blocks were commented-out old implementations, some over three years stale. Git already has that history; the comment doesn't need to.

items.strong: Keep comments next to what they describe
items.text: — a comment two lines above the code it refers to, separated by a blank line, drifts out of sync the first time someone inserts a line between them.

items.strong: Update the comment when you update the code
items.text: — a comment claiming `// returns -1 on error` next to a function that now returns `NULL` on error is worse than no comment at all, because it actively misleads.
— it nests correctly, unlike `/* */`, and is trivially searchable across a codebase with `grep -rn "#if 0"`.

items.strong: Prefix TODOs with a name or ticket ID
items.text: — `// TODO: handle overflow` left anonymous in a shared repo tends to sit untouched for years; `// TODO(rahul, JIRA-4021): handle overflow` gets picked up.

sections.title: Mistakes That Actually Show Up in Real Codebases

items.text: — forgetting the closing `*/` doesn't just break one function; the compiler keeps consuming everything after it as comment text until it finds the next stray `*/` anywhere in the file, or hits end-of-file and reports `error: unterminated comment`.

items.strong: A stray `/` inside a URL comment
items.text: — `// see https://vendor.com/docs/**pinout**` — the `**` sequence right after `docs/` doesn't matter to C, but people writing `/* see https://vendor.com/*docs/*pinout` sometimes accidentally terminate the comment early with an unintended `*/` pattern hiding inside a path segment.

items.strong: Commenting out one half of an if/else
items.text: — disabling just the `if` branch during debugging and leaving a dangling `else` causes a compile error that looks unrelated: `error: expected expression before 'else'`.
— copy-pasting modern example code into a MISRA-C-governed automotive project and having the CI pipeline reject the merge over `-pedantic-errors` with C90 rules is a rite of passage in that industry.

items.q: Q1. Are comments removed by the compiler or the preprocessor?
items.a: The preprocessor removes comments, before the compiler's lexer/parser ever runs. Running `gcc -E file.c` shows the preprocessed output with comments already stripped — proof that they never reach the compilation proper stage.

items.q: Q2. Does C support nested block comments?
items.a: No. `/* */` comments in C are not nestable — the first `*/` encountered closes the comment, regardless of how many `/*` appeared before it. This is different from languages like Rust, which do support nested block comments.

items.q: Q3. In which C standard were // line comments officially introduced?
items.a: C99 (1999). Before that, `//` was a compiler-specific extension in many implementations (borrowed from C++) but not part of the ISO standard. Compiling with `-std=c89 -pedantic-errors` will reject `//` comments with an explicit error.

items.q: Q4. What happens if a block comment is never closed?
items.a: The preprocessor keeps treating everything after the opening `/*` as comment text — including subsequent function definitions — until it finds a `*/` somewhere later in the file, or reaches end-of-file, producing `error: unterminated comment`.

items.q: Q5. Can a comment appear in the middle of a token, like a variable name?
items.a: No — but a comment can appear between tokens without issue, since the preprocessor replaces it with whitespace before tokenizing. `int/*count*/x = 5;` is legal and behaves identically to `int x = 5;` because the comment becomes a token separator.

items.q: Q6. What's the safer alternative to /* */ for temporarily disabling a large block of code?
items.a: `#if 0` ... `#endif`. Unlike `/* */`, it's a preprocessor conditional, not a comment delimiter, so it correctly handles blocks that already contain `/* */` comments without prematurely terminating.

items.q: Q7. Is there a standard documentation-comment syntax in C, like Javadoc in Java?
items.a: No official one exists in the ISO C standard. The de-facto convention across open-source C projects is Doxygen-style comments (`/** ... */` with `@param`/`@return` tags), but tooling support depends entirely on whether the project runs Doxygen — the compiler treats it as an ordinary comment.

items.q: 1. What will `gcc -std=c90 -pedantic-errors` do with a file containing // comments?
items.a: It will refuse to compile, reporting: `error: C++ style comments are not allowed in ISO C90`. Without `-pedantic-errors`, GCC typically accepts `//` as a silent extension even in `-std=c90` mode.

items.q: 2. Predict the output: `int x = 5 /* start */ + 3; printf("%d", x);`
items.a: 8. The comment `/* start */` is removed entirely by the preprocessor before tokenizing, so the compiler sees exactly `int x = 5 + 3;`.

items.q: 3. Given a block comment that contains another /* ... */ inside it, where does the outer comment actually end?
items.a: At the first `*/` encountered — which is the closing of the inner comment, not the outer one. Any code after that point, up until a later `*/`, becomes live code again, often causing confusing syntax errors far from the real problem line.

items.q: 4. Why might `// TODO: fix this later` be considered a poor comment in a shared repository?
items.a: It has no owner and no way to track resolution — anonymous TODOs tend to sit unaddressed indefinitely. A better version includes an author or ticket reference, e.g. `// TODO(priya, TICKET-118): fix rounding for negative inputs`.

items.q: 5. What compiler error would you expect from an unterminated /* comment at the top of a file with several functions below it?
items.a: `error: unterminated comment` — reported once the preprocessor reaches end-of-file still inside the open comment, having silently swallowed every function definition that came after the missing `*/`.

No — it's a preprocessor conditional that evaluates to false, so the code inside is excluded from compilation. It behaves like disabling code (similar effect to commenting it out) but is handled by conditional-compilation logic, which is why it nests correctly where `/* */` does not.

blocks.text: Comments are the one part of C syntax every tutorial claims to have covered in the first ten minutes, and yet the actual failure modes — nesting, the C90/C99 split, unterminated blocks swallowing real code — only show up once you're working in a codebase old enough or strict enough to expose them. Learn the syntax in five minutes; learn the traps by reading this once and remembering them the day your build fails for a reason you can't immediately explain.

If you're setting standards for a team, my honest recommendation: default to // for everything short and inline, reserve /* */ for file headers and Doxygen-style function documentation, and ban commenting-out large blocks in code review in favour of just deleting them — git remembers what you deleted; a stale comment block usually just lies to the next reader.

items.q: Can I use // comments in every C compiler?
items.a: Any compiler supporting C99 or later — which is effectively every modern compiler including GCC and Clang by default — accepts `//`. The exception is code compiled explicitly with `-std=c89`/`-std=c90` plus `-pedantic-errors`, common in legacy embedded and MISRA-C governed projects, where `//` is rejected outright.

items.q: Do comments affect the size or speed of the compiled program?
items.a: No. Comments are removed entirely by the preprocessor before compilation, so they have zero effect on the generated machine code, binary size, or runtime performance — regardless of how many comments a file contains.

To the C compiler, nothing — both are ordinary block comments; the compiler doesn't distinguish the extra asterisk. The `/** */` form is a convention recognized by documentation generators like Doxygen, which treat it as a documentation block to extract into generated docs.

items.q: Why does my commented-out code sometimes cause a compile error instead of being ignored?
items.a: Almost always because the commented block itself contains a `/* */` comment, which prematurely closes the outer comment at its own `*/`. The remaining code becomes active again and usually fails to compile because it's now sitting outside any function. Use `#if 0 ... #endif` instead for blocks that already contain comments.
